approachQuestion.prompt:
Workshop Budget
Start with capital c. Project i requires capital at least need[i] to start and adds positive profit[i] after completion; the requirement is not spent. Complete at most k distinct projects to maximize final capital. Example: c=1, k=2, projects=[(0,2),(2,5),(6,9)] as (need,profit) → 8 by choosing profits 2 then 5.

1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ k ≤ n; 0 ≤ c,need[i] ≤ 1000000000; 1 ≤ profit[i] ≤ 1000000000. Capital fits signed 64 bits. Input is read-only and unsorted. Return only final capital. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ k ≤ n; 0 ≤ c,need[i] ≤ 1000000000; 1 ≤ profit[i] ≤ 1000000000. Capital fits signed 64 bits. Input is read-only and unsorted. Return only final capital.

options.text: Sort a copy by required capital. Before each choice, push profits of all newly affordable projects into a max-heap. Remove its maximum, add that profit to capital, and repeat up to k times; stop if no project is affordable.
options.feedback: Among affordable projects, a larger profit cannot make any later choice less affordable. Exchanging it for a smaller first choice therefore preserves future eligibility and gives at least as much capital.

options.text: Before each choice, scan all unchosen projects for the largest affordable profit.
options.feedback: This makes the same valid choices but repeatedly revisits projects whose eligibility has not changed.

options.text: Sort all projects by profit descending and take the first k without checking requirements.
options.feedback: In the example, profit 9 is not initially affordable.

options.text: Among affordable projects choose the one with the lowest requirement, regardless of profit.
options.feedback: With c=1,k=1, projects [(0,1),(1,9)], this gets 2 instead of 10.

details: Sort a copy by required capital. Before each choice, push profits of all newly affordable projects into a max-heap. Remove its maximum, add that profit to capital, and repeat up to k times; stop if no project is affordable.

Required capital is an affordability threshold, not money deducted for taking a project. Add every newly affordable project, then take the greatest profit. Choosing by smallest requirement alone may waste a limited project slot.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A with iterative heapsort on a copied n-record array and a binary max-heap. Let n be projects and 1≤k≤n. An eligibility pointer moves only forward; there is no hashing. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(k log(k+1)) time, O(k) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Sort thresholds and insert each affordable project at most once.
details: Comparison sorting is O(n log(n+1)). Every project is inserted at most once and at most k are removed; k≤n keeps all heap work within the sorting bound. The copy and affordable heap each use O(n) storage. Requirements are thresholds, not deductions; only profits change capital.
“O(kn) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This describes repeated scans and omits the input copy used by A.
“O(n+k) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Sorting and variable-sized heap repairs are not linear.
“O(k log(k+1)) time, O(k) auxiliary space”: Even k=1 can require examining and sorting n projects; eligible heap size can be n.
